I think Firebase was kind of douchebags assuming the story is correct, if you change how people are billed you should give people time to adjust their software.

Yet another example that Google so far doesn't get the public cloud... E.g. shutdown Prediction APIs, charge 70x, not enough support. I believe Google got much better tech than AWS, but the culture, support and strategy has blind spots.
there is no way to cap your billing on gcp. you can get notifications but that's it. i don't want to get throttled below my quota but some type of spend limit would be good.

That's standard for Firebase apps. It's also recommended by Google (they describe the keys as 'public by design').' (referring to Firebase API keys being exposed client-side, later exploited via Gemini access)

This is awesome. I built a real time whiteboarding app for teachers over 10 years ago on the backbone of the original Firebase service. It was so fast I was able to build basic collision physics... What a shame to be killed by Google.

One of the things I find quite nice about firebase is the quite powerful separation between the logic of data retrieval/update and the enforcement of access policy... you can build the prototype on a happy path with barely any authorization enforcement and then add it later and have quite complete confidence.
Finally, waiting for something along the lines of these. Firebase is kind of the poster child for vendor lock in, and has been around for a long time. It's time we have some healthy competition.
How do the querying features compare to Firebase? Firebase is notorious for having an unintuitive lack of server-side query options when you start using it.

Besides the pricing, the other painful thing about Firebase are the storage rules. Given I understand you want to give maximum control to frontend developers without having a backend, the fact that I need to reimplement them if I switch serverless is an absolute pain.
After being both delighted and frustrated about Firebase I decided that something must be done. The developer experience on Firebase is awesome but the tech and the lock-in effect is super bad.

I am a strong believer that Firebase model is the way forward... what makes Firebase special is the glue they use: Account management and libraries come for free... Firebase is not just Firestore, it is a set of tools that work together seamlessly.

I am ecstatic that someone is finally taking on Firebase. As a Firebase user, I find it invaluable. Their free plan and limits are very generous... Following this intently, because Firebase has no true competitor.

I use Firebase and find it easy, useful and constantly improving (cloud functions etc.). Their support, however, is a joke. 5 questions can be logged per year for one-on-one email support and then you're on your own.

We've also gone from ~$25/mo to $1000-2000/mo with the pricing change. While it's not the end of the world... there's also been 3-4 incidents of downtime (> 1 hour) in the last 2 months, with no way to contact anyone except their stupid web form.

They have no phone number to contact, no way to dispute this other than email — which they have ignored us for over a month now without replying to our continued requests. Trapped. Doomed. We have no further options.
having mixed feelings, on one hand I'm super happy that Firebase has grown to where it is now, the product has always been awesome... I often think of Firebase team members as friends and teachers.

I've been watching your journey since Envolve. We were one of the first hundred users to join Firebase (ID:68) and I remember how easy it took to add real time notifications to one of my product (5 hrs I believe).

We've been using the Firebase platform for a while now... I must say that their system has been one of the best we have used in a longtime... One area that I'd like to see improved though is a deeper querying language for database.
When will it support a count query? now to be able to count number of children I have to download all the data. Count is such an important feature for me.
